data.title: Wine and Dine Festival vendors report Halloween boost in sales and footfall
data.description:
Vendors at Hong Kong’s Wine and Dine Festival reported a stronger turnout and signs of improving business on Saturday as the annual event entered its first weekend, coinciding with Halloween celebrations and extended opening hours until 1am.
Some exhibitors said visitor numbers had increased noticeably compared with the first two days of the four-day festival, while others expressed cautious optimism about sales amid a challenging retail environment.
Henry Leung, a staff member at food and beverage importer Unicube, said business at his booth was about 20 per cent higher than at the same time last year, with the evening’s peak expected after 8pm.
“There are more people. Just look at our booth, we have customers coming in groups,” he said, adding that Saturday had been busier than Thursday and Friday.
But he also pointed to pressure such as the greater cross-border connectivity weighing on local retail by spreading consumer spending across different destinations, even as he reported seeing more mainland Chinese visitors at the festival.
Leung said Halloween had helped create a livelier atmosphere, with more visitors expected to arrive in costume as the evening progressed.
Michelle Chan, 29, an office employee, visited the festival with three friends after dinner and planned to spend about HK$500 (US$64) on wine and snacks.
“We thought we’d do something different for Halloween this year instead of going to Lan Kwai Fong,” she said. “It’s nice to have somewhere outdoors where we can have a few drinks, try different wines and enjoy the harbour view.”
Chan said the extended opening hours were an added attraction, as her group did not have to rush through the festival.
“We’ll probably stay until around midnight. It’s Saturday anyway, so there’s no hurry to go home,” she said.
Charmaine Suen, executive secretary at EcceVino, a European wine importer exhibiting at the Grand Wine Pavilion, also said the atmosphere was better than last year, with noticeably more people attending.
Suen, whose company has operated in Hong Kong for more than a decade and specialises primarily in Italian wines, praised organisers for improving the festival’s surrounding environment and facilities.
She suggested that government efforts to stimulate the economy might have contributed to the more upbeat atmosphere.
Asked whether Hong Kong consumers had become more knowledgeable about wine, Suen said their understanding had been relatively sophisticated for years.
Organised by the Hong Kong Tourism Board, the festival returned to the Central Harbourfront Event Space and Tamar Park on Thursday with more than 340 booths, an increase of more than 10 per cent from last year, showcasing wines and food from around 31 countries and regions.
For the first time, Friday and Saturday opening hours were extended until 1am, an hour later than in previous years, offering visitors more time to enjoy the waterfront festivities.
The event also coincided with Halloween weekend this year, giving organisers an opportunity to attract evening revellers alongside wine enthusiasts and food lovers.
New attractions include a coffee garden at Tamar Park featuring 13 coffee brands, creative coffee cocktails and live performances, as well as three guided wine walks introducing participants to different wine regions, grape varieties and food pairings.
More than 20 wine masterclasses were also being held, while the Grand Wine Pavilion featured premium selections from renowned regions including Bordeaux and Burgundy.
Saturday’s programme included a free tasting of a 2014 Clos de Vougeot Grand Cru Burgundy wine during a sunset session, alongside special offers on selected premium wines.
The festival runs until Sunday, when special dining experiences featuring European cheeses and contemporary interpretations of Hong Kong cuisine will round off the four-day event.
Admission costs HK$40 for adults and HK$20 for children aged three to 11, while tasting tokens cost HK$25 each.

data.title: Halloween revellers told to avoid Lan Kwai Fong as crowds pack streets
data.description:
Hong Kong’s inaugural “Halloween Month” has been a boon for businesses, with bar and restaurant operators in Lan Kwai Fong expecting big sales on Saturday, but by 7.30pm police were urging revellers to celebrate elsewhere as the area was packed.
With Halloween falling on a weekend this year, businesses were expecting a bumper turnout as the Tourism Board’s inaugural campaign for the celebrations wrapped up. Operators noted a surge in visitors from mainland Chinese cities in the Greater Bay Area.
“It’s been very well received by everybody,” said Anthea Cheung So-may, director of the Lan Kwai Fong Association, on Saturday. “People are really happy to see this celebration.”
The campaign, which began on October 17, involves street celebrations in Central, including Lan Kwai Fong, Kai Tak, Mong Kok and Tsim Sha Tsui East on three consecutive Saturdays, culminating on Halloween night.
The South China Morning Post observed that some eager revellers were already dressed up and drinking as early as noon in some parts of the city on Saturday.
Peel Street, which has become another popular Halloween party spot in Central, was bustling by 5pm, with costumed revellers dancing in the street as music played.
The streets of Lan Kwai Fong were packed as early as 6.30pm. City workers hastily erected steel barriers along streets in Central as thousands of costumed revellers slowly snaked their way to the party neighbourhood.
Police were out in large numbers, with at least a dozen vehicles parked along Lyndhurst Terrace and officers manning every nearby street. By evening, crowds were being instructed to move in a single direction.
While many party-goers stuck with traditional spooky costumes, others dressed as gold Buddhas, Lipton iced tea cartons, Ronald McDonald and TV show character Wednesday Addams.
Among the thousands in Lan Kwai Fong were 23-year-old classmates Cathy Kai Yi and Thea Cheng Xi, who were dressed as bottles of mustard and ketchup.

The pair, who are from Henan province and moved to the city two months ago to study for postgraduate degrees at Polytechnic University, were marking their first Halloween in the city.
“It’s so interesting,” Kai said. “There’s so many people wearing so many different outfits.
“It’s a totally new experience for us,” she added, noting that there was nothing similar in her home province.
Kai said they would try to stay in the area for about two hours, but they planned to mostly take photos rather than spend money in bars.
She said she would “absolutely” tell her friends back home to visit Hong Kong for Halloween.
Cheung, of the Lan Kwai Fong Association, said that business had increased by as much as 40 per cent over the last two weeks compared with previous years, with people dressing up far earlier.
Tens of thousands of people had snaked their way through the narrow streets of Central over the last few weekends, she said, noting one-way traffic flows were implemented as early as 7.30pm on Friday.
“For tonight, because it’s the final night of the Halloween celebrations, I expect the sales increase will be more than 50 per cent … year on year,” she said. “We are very confident about this number.”

Alongside an influx of international visitors, Cheung also said there had been a noticeable increase in revellers coming from the bay area, which she attributed to convenient border crossings.
The month-long campaign forms part of a tourism strategy outlined in February’s budget to place greater emphasis on festivals that are less prominent on the mainland, including Halloween.
Timothy Chui Ting-pong, executive director of the Hong Kong Tourism Association, said business had been “very brisk” over the course of the campaign.
“Young people living in the bay area are very engaged with Hong Kong’s Halloween celebrations, which has directly pushed up the number of visitors coming to Hong Kong,” he said.
Apart from Lan Kwai Fong, Central’s Statue Square Gardens is hosting illuminated installations alongside a large costume party on Chater Road.
Across Victoria Harbour in Kowloon, Tsim Sha Tsui East was hosting a grand Halloween gala, while parts of Mong Kok were transformed into a large-scale cosplay carnival.

data.title: Hong Kong may raise GDP forecast as growth poised for 5-year high: Paul Chan
data.description:
Hong Kong’s economic growth this year could be the city’s strongest in five years, with potential for further upward revisions after the full-year forecast was previously raised to a range of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent, the finance chief has said.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Saturday that the city’s economy grew by 5.1 per cent in the first half of the year, driven by strong export momentum and investment growth.
“Although the third-quarter figures have not yet been released, I can share that exports remained very strong in the quarter,” he told a radio programme.
He said the strong momentum was coupled with a high volume of visitors to Hong Kong as the city hosted a variety of events such as the Wine and Dine Festival.
The coming Fintech Week would draw more visitors, while the Global Financial Leaders’ Investment Summit would gather at least 120 presidents and CEOs from financial organisations worldwide, he said.
“This year, 2026, has the potential to deliver the strongest full-year economic growth in the past five years,” he said, adding that the full-year growth forecast could be raised further.
“We’ve been keeping a close eye on the figures and tracking changes and trends. Overall this year, not just in the third quarter, but heading into the fourth quarter as well, the momentum remains quite strong.”
In August, authorities raised the city’s full-year economic growth forecast for 2026 to a range of 3.5 to 4.5 per cent following a 4.3 per cent expansion in the second quarter, supported by buoyant external trade and resilient domestic demand.
The forecast was revised from the previous range of 2.5 to 3.5 per cent, with the government citing a stronger-than-expected performance in the first half of the year and taking into account the near-term outlook.
The economy expanded by 5.1 per cent in the first half, its strongest half-yearly performance in nearly five years.
Exports of goods surged by 28.9 per cent year on year in real terms, while private consumption expenditure rose by 2.8 per cent and overall investment increased by 4.4 per cent.
On the tourism front, the city received 26.71 million visitors in the first half of this year, a 13 per cent increase from a year earlier.
In particular, the momentum in exports continued in the second half of the year.
According to data revealed on Wednesday, the city’s exports jumped by 64.9 per cent year on year in September to HK$762.6 billion (US$97.8 billion), the highest growth in more than 40 years, with artificial intelligence-related products further fuelling the momentum of recent months.
The government had earlier said September marked the 20th consecutive month of double-digit growth and the fastest monthly year-on-year increase in more than four decades.
Chan said the government would continue to foster steady economic growth, noting that while the inflation rate was influenced by oil prices, the increase had remained relatively modest, and price levels remained stable.
But he added that geopolitical factors continued to pose risks, fuelling oil prices and inflationary pressures, while interest rates that were expected to remain high into next year could put pressure on both the property market and the broader economy.
“We remain highly vigilant regarding the financial risks, and we also urge everyone to remain cautious about risks across all aspects of their investments,” he said.
Asked whether the government would offer more sweeteners in next year’s budget, Chan said authorities would do their best depending on economic indicators, but he noted that future infrastructure expenditure would be substantial, requiring an approach of “spending where necessary and exercising fiscal prudence”.
Gary Ng Cheuk-yan, a senior economist at Natixis Corporate and Investment Bank, said Hong Kong’s full-year growth this year would likely reach 4.4 per cent based on the current trajectory, which was “very close” to the current government’s forecast.
He said authorities might increase the range from the revised 3.5 to 4.5 per cent further to 4 to 5 per cent.
“In the last quarter, global AI demand will continue to fuel the semiconductor super cycle and support exports,” he said.
“However, there are persisting headwinds from private consumption, especially with challenges from a weaker wealth effect from stock markets, job creation and elevated interest rates.”
Additional reporting by Wynna Wong

data.title: As battery wars intensify, China’s CATL seeks growth beyond its core business
data.description:
Contemporary Amperex Technology Ltd (CATL) has doubled down on new businesses including battery swapping and energy storage as the world’s largest battery maker seeks new growth drivers amid intensifying price wars and mounting pressure on profitability.
But the new path is far from straightforward. Established players like Nio have already built a strong presence in battery swapping, while BYD has reinforced its position in energy-storage systems.
Lucas Zhang Liutong, director of Hong Kong-based consultancy WaterRock Energy Economics, said competition in both sectors was “already quite intense”.
To maintain its leadership, CATL needed to evolve beyond being a battery cell manufacturer and become “a standard-setting platform” with a more integrated ecosystem, Zhang added.
The firm, based in southeastern China’s Fujian province, has announced four strategic battery-swapping partnerships with car manufacturers this month, including China’s central state-owned Dongfeng Motor Corporation and Huawei Technologies subsidiary Shenzhen Yinwang Intelligent Technology.
Battery swapping, which powers an electric vehicle (EV) by physically replacing a depleted battery with a fully charged one in three to five minutes, has emerged as a major alternative to BYD-led “flash charging” technology, which can replenish batteries to near-full levels in less than 10 minutes.
Chinese vehicle makers are racing to attract petrol-car owners amid a growth slowdown in the EV market.
Nio, known for its long-term commitment to battery swapping, has also formed partnerships with CGN New Energy Holdings and Geely Holding, the parent of Geely Auto, to expand the technology’s adoption.
Notably, Geely was CATL’s largest customer in August, accounting for 9.6 per cent of the month’s total battery supply, according to a report by the China Passenger Car Association released in September.


Meanwhile, CATL recently established a new wholly owned energy-storage technology subsidiary with registered capital of 5 billion yuan (US$750 million), with business plans that include the development of artificial intelligence software.
Internationally, the firm announced on Tuesday a new 3 gigawatt-hour sodium-ion battery project with Intilion, a German provider of energy storage solutions.
BYD, China’s second-largest EV battery maker after CATL, has also accelerated the overseas expansion of its energy-storage business. Construction began on its Polish project in late September, just three months after the agreement was signed.
The shift towards energy storage reflects a broader industry trend towards a higher-growth and more visible market segment.
Demand from AI data centres for stable power supply remained a key driver of growth in global battery energy-storage system orders, despite the sector’s still modest share of overall electricity consumption, said Yang Jing, director of Asia-Pacific corporate ratings at Fitch Ratings.
The move into new businesses also came as analysts warned that persistent price wars in mainland China could erode CATL’s fundamentals if exports of EV batteries and its higher-margin energy-storage operations failed to make a larger contribution to fourth-quarter earnings, according to a note by Morgan Stanley published this week.
CATL’s sharp slowdown in third-quarter profit growth has already dragged its Hong Kong-listed shares to a record low since their debut, as investors worry that China’s resumed battery consumption tax, a reduction in export tax rebates and rising overseas trade barriers could weigh on the company’s performance.
Nomura analyst Ethan Zhang said the new tax burden could hurt CATL’s unit profitability in the near term, cutting his earnings forecasts for 2026 to 2028 by as much as 10.2 per cent, according to a note on October 20.
The battery giant also acknowledged that it was discussing ways to share the tax burden with carmakers, according to notes from its October 20 earnings call seen by the South China Morning Post.
Fitch’s Yang, however, projected that CATL’s profitability could be nearing a bottom, with deliveries shifting towards higher-margin products and the effects of renegotiated customer contracts beginning to take hold after the fourth quarter.

data.title: Appeal for private flight to bring critically ill British baby home from Hong Kong
data.description:
A UK-registered air ambulance and family support charity has issued an urgent appeal for a donated private flight to bring a critically ill baby boy home from Hong Kong.
Lia’s Wings said on Friday that nine-month-old Matthew, from Nottinghamshire, had travelled to Hong Kong with his mother several months ago to visit relatives.
He fell ill with influenza A and suffered three cardiac arrests, leaving him critically ill in hospital. His brain was reportedly deprived of oxygen for 47 minutes.
His mother, Sophia Lee, approached Lia’s Wings as a last resort, hoping the charity could arrange an air transfer to bring him home for medical care.
The charity said on social media that Matthew’s travel insurer would not cover the cost of his journey home and that commercial airlines had deemed him too high-risk to fly.
It added that an air ambulance was an option, but the cost of up to HK$2.1 million (US$267,993) was beyond what the charity and his family could afford.
Lia’s Wings said it was now exploring what might be its last option, appealing to the aviation industry for a donated private flight to bring Matthew home safely.
“Without the repatriation, he risks becoming a tragedy, a British baby left somewhere where he wasn’t within the reach of the help of the community where he belongs to,” Charlotte Young, the chief operating officer of Lia’s Wings, said.
“Commercial airlines are very used to adults, but babies bring a whole new level of concern for them.
“We tried to have that as a first option, because it would have made everything more financially viable, a fifth of the cost, but it is not an option, although we tried our hardest.”
Matthew is reportedly “incredibly unwell” but in a stable condition.

data.title: As Hong Kong releases full report on Tai Po fire, here’s all you need to know
data.description:
We have put together 10 stories from our coverage on the full report of the Wang Fuk Court fire, released almost a year since the tragedy claimed 168 lives. If you would like to see more of our reporting, please consider subscribing.
1. John Lee apologises for Tai Po fire, unveils reforms as housing chief resigns
Hong Kong’s leader has apologised for last year’s deadly Tai Po fire, vowing extensive civil service and legislative reforms and an overhaul of government departments as his housing chief Winnie Ho Wing-yin resigned to offer political accountability.
2. ‘Why did it take 11 months?’: apology too late for some Tai Po fire survivors
Hong Kong officials’ apology over the deadly Tai Po blaze nearly a year ago came too late, residents of the fire-ravaged estate have said, as they urged authorities to learn from the disaster and pursue long-term reforms.
3. Lit cigarette, combustibles and ‘human fault’ led to deadly Hong Kong fire: report

A combination of a lit cigarette and an “abundant fuel” of combustible materials caused Hong Kong’s deadliest fire in decades, according to a long-awaited report which found the blaze would not have killed so many people, or happened at all, without “human fault”.
4. Housing chief resigns, government admits ‘decades of failure’ led to Tai Po fire – as it happened
The report, released 11 months after the Wang Fuk Court fire in Tai Po claimed 168 lives, assigned blame to the main contractor for renovations at the housing estate, the project consultant and an inspector for their alleged roles in the tragedy. It also singled out four government departments for accountability.
5. Lee to stay on, says housing minister’s resignation his ‘political decision’

Hong Kong’s leader has said the housing minister’s resignation was his “comprehensive political decision” in establishing accountability for the city’s deadliest fire in decades, with a three-member team to also investigate up to 50 civil servants.
6. Chain of failures: 5 key takeaways from report on Tai Po blaze

Here are the key takeaways from the report by a judge-led independent committee and a government press conference on the findings.
7. Hong Kong to replace disgraced housing unit over deadly Tai Po fire
Hong Kong’s disgraced Independent Checking Unit (ICU) will be disbanded as part of reforms in the wake of the city’s deadliest fire in decades, after a judge-led inquiry identified it as the government arm with the greatest responsibility for the Wang Fuk Court inferno.
8. Departments ‘passed the ball’ on safety complaints, leaving residents helpless
No government department took effective ownership of fire safety risks ahead of the deadly Tai Po fire in Hong Kong, allowing complaints made by residents to fall into a vacuum, according to an independent committee.
9. Hong Kong ministers defend decision not to resign over deadly Tai Po fire
Ministers have defended their decision not to step down over the deadly Tai Po fire, insisting they are putting Hong Kong’s well-being ahead of personal considerations.
10. Security chief vows his task force will root out bid-rigging in Hong Kong

Hong Kong’s security chief has expressed confidence that a new joint task force led by him will eradicate the decades-long problem of bid-rigging, while denying that the reforms came too late after the deadly Tai Po fire.

data.title: China joins global race to reawaken brain-injury patients through ultrasound therapy
data.description:
After spending three months in a coma following a brain haemorrhage, a patient in China has regained the ability to speak, eat and walk with support – part of an early clinical trial using targeted sound waves to help “wake up” severely damaged brains, according to state media.
The technology, developed by a coalition including the Chinese Academy of Sciences’ Shenzhen Institutes of Advanced Technology, used focused ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep within the brain without requiring invasive surgery or implanted electrodes, state broadcaster CCTV reported earlier this week.
It was presented at a brain-computer interface (BCI) industry conference that opened in Shenzhen earlier this month. While public attention around BCIs often centres on controlling computers or robotic limbs, the research showcased efforts to apply such technologies to neurological rehabilitation.
The technique uses magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) to identify target zones, especially the thalamus, which plays a critical role in awareness and communication between neural networks. By directing focused ultrasound pulses towards these regions, researchers seek to restore brain networks essential to consciousness.
In a preliminary study conducted alongside Kunming Medical University, 13 out of 24 patients with chronic disorders of consciousness showed improvements in conscious behaviour, according to CCTV. They received three 20-minute sessions per week over four weeks.
In one notable case, a patient who had spent three months in a coma following a brain bleed was able to have conversations again, feed himself and walk with help after 30 days of ultrasound therapy and rehabilitation.
However, the CCTV report did not indicate whether the trial included a control group, which could limit the conclusions that can be drawn.


The televised findings followed an earlier peer-reviewed case study published by the same research group in Frontiers in Psychiatry in February. Tracking a single patient treated with focused ultrasound, the team documented a “progressive and clinically significant behavioural recovery, ultimately emerging from the minimally conscious state”.
But the researchers cautioned that the findings from one patient could not be generalised without broader, controlled studies.
Focused ultrasound has attracted interest because of its ability to reach deep brain structures without the risks associated with craniotomy or surgical implants. The ambition to restore consciousness through ultrasound is starting to gain momentum worldwide.
In the United States, a multicentre clinical trial led by the University of California, Los Angeles, is recruiting 60 patients with severe brain injuries. The study includes a sham-stimulation control group to confirm whether any improvements come directly from the medical intervention rather than from spontaneous recovery.
Commercial interest in ultrasound-based brain interfaces is also growing.
In September, Merge Labs, whose co-founders include OpenAI’s Sam Altman and California Institute of Technology bioengineer Mikhail Shapiro, partnered with US medical device firm Butterfly Network to develop the technology.
Merge said it was exploring how molecular technologies and ultrasound could be used to communicate with neurons.

data.title: After brutal sell-off, what comes next for the titans of Big Tech?
data.description:
Soaring artificial intelligence revenues have failed to shield Intel, Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet from a brutal Wall Street sell-off, as their latest quarterly results deepened investor jitters over mounting capital spending and delayed returns.
Intel plunged about 23 per cent in extended trading on Thursday, while Amazon shed 7.3 per cent. Alphabet tumbled 12.6 per cent during the regular session in its worst day on record, dragging the Nasdaq Composite down 1.4 per cent and sliding slightly further after hours.
Their earnings reports exposed the precarious economics of the AI boom: hyperscalers are racing to build out advanced computing capacity well before those assets generate enough cash to finance the next wave of infrastructure.
With both Alphabet and Amazon signalling even larger capital expenditure in 2027, any slower-than-expected top-line growth threatens to squeeze liquidity while depreciation and operational costs pile up.
Ahead of the financial results, Melissa Otto, global head at S&P Visible Alpha Research, warned on Wednesday that cloud giants’ spending was “projected to outpace revenue growth in the near term”, potentially weighing on free cash flow.
Alphabet burns cash despite cloud surge
Alphabet’s Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to US$30.7 billion, while group operating profit rose by 30 per cent. But capital expenditure of US$51.4 billion outpaced operating cash flow of US$42.3 billion, leaving a quarterly free cash outflow of US$9.1 billion.
While free cash flow remained positive on a trailing 12-month basis, this marked the US giant’s second consecutive quarter recording negative free cash flow.
Liquidity was further constrained by a US$5.2 billion European Commission antitrust fine and inventory commitments for tensor processing units, which Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said were backed by signed customer contracts.
Alphabet maintained its full-year capital expenditure forecast of US$195 billion to US$205 billion. Finance chief Anat Ashkenazi warned spending would rise substantially in 2027, driving up depreciation costs, while greater use of third-party computing infrastructure would pressure near-term cloud margins.
Compounding the pressure, core search growth slowed to 12 per cent year on year, down from 17 per cent in the second quarter and 19 per cent in the first.
While chief business officer Philipp Schindler blamed currency swings and the lower monetisation of Google AI Mode queries for the deceleration from the second quarter, the numbers fed into worries that the firm’s main revenue engine is losing momentum as online users turn to AI to search for information.
Amazon defends record capital demands
Amazon struck a parallel chord of operational strength eclipsed by capital needs. Amazon Web Services (AWS) revenue grew 39.3 per cent to US$46 billion, its fastest expansion in nearly five years, propelling its group operating margin to a record 13.9 per cent.
Yet heavy AI investment drained cash balances. Amazon posted a US$42.4 billion free cash outflow for the 12 months ending September 30, reversing a US$14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, even as operating cash flow rose 29 per cent to US$168.3 billion.
The company held its full-year cash capital expenditure guidance at about US$220 billion. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy signalled that 2027 spending would be “meaningfully more”, while pushing back against investor scepticism, saying: “We can fund this plan.”
While AWS revenue exceeded consensus estimates, it missed the 42 per cent threshold anticipated by the most bullish analysts. Looking past the near-term cash burn, Jassy projected AWS growth would exceed 40 per cent across both 2027 and 2028.
Intel hit by forecast miss and plant disruptions
Intel faced a distinct set of operational headwinds, issuing fourth-quarter guidance that missed Wall Street targets across the board. The chipmaker projected revenue of US$15 billion to US$16 billion and adjusted earnings per share of 25 US cents, well below the consensus forecasts of US$17 billion and 43 US cents cited by Goldman Sachs.
While third-quarter sales in Intel’s data centre and AI unit surged 78 per cent, revenue in its Client Computing and Physical AI Group, which includes personal computer chips, fell 5 per cent. Management said higher memory prices and limited enterprise IT budgets were denting PC demand, projecting a 10 per cent decline in global PC shipments in 2027.
Manufacturing and packaging constraints also capped server-chip deliveries. An accident at its Kiryat Gat fabrication facility in Israel was expected to shave fourth-quarter revenue by about US$300 million, with a similar drag likely in the subsequent quarter, Intel said.
Microsoft defies the hyperscaler cash drain
Microsoft, on the other hand, appeared more adept at funding heavy infrastructure out of its operations than its Big Tech peers.
Microsoft Azure revenue rose 48 per cent as operating cash flow hit US$58 billion. That comfortably absorbed US$39.4 billion in property and equipment spending, leaving the software giant with US$18.6 billion in free cash flow for the September quarter.
Chief financial officer Amy Hood reiterated that Microsoft expected to stay free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. She noted that December-quarter capital outlays would eclipse US$50 billion, inclusive of finance leases. Some third-party capacity deliveries had shifted to the fiscal second half.

data.title: New renovation body may offer bigger subsidies for ageing Hong Kong districts
data.description:
Hong Kong’s planned renovation monitoring body will consider larger subsidies for homeowners of ageing buildings in older districts or with high elderly populations who use its supervision services for major repairs, the finance chief has said.
Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said on Saturday that the Building Maintenance Support and Services Council, set up to curb malpractice in the industry after the Tai Po fire report, would be non-profit but would have to recover its costs, since owners mainly bear responsibility for maintaining private residential property.
He said service charges would depend on factors such as the scope of the work, with fees estimated at several thousand Hong Kong dollars per household, but that authorities would subsidise those in need.
“In places with a high elderly population, and in older districts and ageing buildings, there’s no harm in offering a larger subsidy when appropriate,” he told a radio programme.
“The most important thing is to get this work done promptly to ensure everyone’s living environment is safe and comfortable. In this regard, if there is a further need for additional financial support, we are more than happy to provide it.”
On Thursday, authorities announced that the government would establish the council as part of the reforms following an independent committee’s report on the devastating blaze at Wang Fuk Court in Tai Po last November, which killed 168 people.
The report found that substandard materials used in the estate’s renovation at the time had contributed to the rapid spread of the fire, and that evidence showed “numerous features” of the project bore the hallmarks of bid-rigging and anticompetitive conduct.
The council will assign inspection consultants to property owners, handle tendering and assessments for supervision consultants and contractors, and regularly evaluate performance to uphold project quality.
Authorities said HK$300 million (US$38.24 million) had been earmarked for the initiative, comprising HK$100 million in start-up capital and HK$200 million in subsidies for homeowners.

Asked about the subsidy ratio, Chan said it would be inappropriate to set a uniform threshold and that flexibility was needed, given the varying scale of individual residential developments.
“There are some older buildings with a lot of elderly residents living in them. To encourage them to go ahead with it, and also because the risks there are even higher, if we offer a higher subsidy ratio for those cases, I believe everyone would be fine with that,” he said.
“In some districts that might be older but are still quite expensive, the homeowners there are relatively well-off. For those cases, providing professional support and guidance is more important than giving financial aid.”
Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on Saturday that about 650 applications had been received across the three pre-qualification lists for inspection consultants, supervision consultants and contractors.
The lists for inspection consultants and supervision consultants had each received about 150 applications, while the contractors’ list had received about 350.
“It is roughly two to three times higher than the previous lists. The figure shows that more people in the industry have stepped forward and are willing to submit for our pre-qualification, which is a positive sign,” she said.
“If more people take part and competition increases, coupled with our new council acting as a gatekeeper, I believe there will be much greater assurance regarding the reasonableness of prices for our future major renovation projects.”
She said she expected the council to recruit about 100 staff by the middle of next year, including professionals and administrative personnel.
Also as part of the reforms, the disgraced Independent Checking Unit (ICU), which the report identified as the government arm most responsible for the lack of oversight of Wang Fuk Court’s renovation, will be replaced by a new Public Housing Building Control Section.
Deputy Financial Secretary Michael Wong Wai-lun said the new body was not merely a renamed version of the unit but a drive for fundamental institutional reform to rectify past shortcomings.
He said a dedicated team would be established and a designated liaison officer assigned to each regulatory project to ensure all complaints were properly addressed.
He added that authorities had so far bought the ownership rights of nearly 95 per cent of Wang Fuk Court flats under the government buyout scheme.
The remaining ownership rights would be restored through legislative means next year, he said, but that process would not start yet because authorities were still handling acquisitions from some residents while others were choosing flats, to avoid sending mixed messages.

data.title: Beijing rejects spy claims involving Nvidia CEO amid rising US-China tech tensionsMegaspeed has previously come under US scrutiny over suspicions that the company was helping China circumvent US expor
data.description:
China on Friday hit out at reported US intelligence allegations that a suspected Chinese spy had targeted Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang, dismissing the claims as “groundless speculation” aimed at smearing Beijing.
“The relevant report is based on groundless speculation and [is] purely aimed at smearing and slandering China,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun told a regular media briefing in Beijing.
The pushback came after US outlet The New York Times reported on Thursday that US intelligence agencies had identified a Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, as a suspected Chinese asset who had approached and tried to develop a close business relationship with the Nvidia chief.
US agencies believed that Huang, an executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed, had been passing information to Beijing, according to the report. The two Huangs are not related.
Megaspeed had previously come under US scrutiny over suspicions that the company was helping China circumvent US export controls on advanced semiconductors, the report said, citing anonymous officials with access to classified intelligence.
The news report also said US officials initially believed Nvidia’s Huang was unaware of the woman’s alleged intelligence activities, while no evidence showed that the Nvidia chief had knowingly shared sensitive information with her.

The allegations come amid heightened US scrutiny of chip exports to China, as Washington seeks to restrict Beijing’s access to premium chips critical to training advanced artificial intelligence models, citing national security concerns.
In a statement to the South China Morning Post on Friday, an Nvidia representative said that “Megaspeed has been no different than many other regional cloud customers” and that “Jensen’s interactions with Ms. Huang are not unusual or unexpected”, as meetings with customers were part of a CEO’s job.
The company added that “the diversion allegations against this regional cloud were thoroughly investigated and debunked last year”, according to the statement.
Megaspeed did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Friday.
Once a major market for Nvidia, China has become increasingly difficult for the US chip giant to navigate, as Washington’s tightening export controls on advanced AI chips have severely restricted its sales to the country.
Meanwhile, Chinese chipmakers from Huawei Technologies to Moore Threads, among others, are gaining ground on Nvidia as Beijing accelerates efforts to achieve semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Beijing-based Moore Threads, often hailed as China’s “little Nvidia”, reported on Wednesday a nearly 1,774 per cent surge in third-quarter revenue to 1.55 billion yuan (US$232.4 million). It attributed the gain to robust domestic demand for graphics processing units used for AI model training and inference across cloud providers, telecommunications operators and computing centres.

data.title: One AI rule book: chip expert urges shared standards across China, US models
data.description:
The co-founder of Chinese chip giant Cambricon Technologies urged the introduction of universal ethical requirements for leading Chinese and American artificial intelligence models on Friday to mitigate growing risks to society.
Chen Yunji’s remarks at an event in Shanghai come as the rapid advance of AI systems globally has resulted in a string of high-profile cyberattacks that have threatened critical infrastructure and breached government servers.
Predicting that AI advances would develop even faster, Chen proposed a universal “ethics checker” that all leading AI models would need to satisfy, citing the systems developed by Chinese companies DeepSeek and ByteDance as well as American start-up OpenAI.
“All human beings and nations would need to agree on this ethics checker … to prevent these large language models from doing harm to human beings in the future,” he said at a panel on AI safety and risks on the opening day of the World Laureates Forum in Shanghai’s Lingang Special Area.
One of China’s leading chip experts, Chen is a professor at the Chinese Academy of Sciences. He founded Cambricon Technologies in 2016 with his brother, Chen Tianshi, helping the company grow into one of China’s hottest domestic chip designers, with a market capitalisation of over 600 billion yuan (US$90 billion).
Warning that humanity could soon face AI systems capable of autonomously improving themselves in a process known as “recursive self-improvement” (RSI), Chen said it might be impossible to completely prevent harm, given the opaque nature of AI decision-making.
However, he said he had “faith” that RSI could be made safe by leveraging AI itself at each stage of development to monitor and safeguard the more powerful systems that would follow.
There is no way to stop AI in the current world, where there is too much economic and military motivation to go full speed ahead
Martin Hellman, Turing Award recipient
Beijing has signalled growing concerns over the cyber-hacking capabilities of AI models in recent weeks. Earlier this month, it proposed export controls on advanced AI systems, with additional restrictions for those that cross critical cyber-hacking thresholds.
On Thursday, US cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike said in a report that an unidentified group had used an open-source DeepSeek model and another unidentified model to conduct cyberattacks against more than 200 organisations worldwide since October 17.
DeepSeek did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Martin Hellman, the American cryptologist and Turing Award recipient who also spoke at the forum on Friday, said the latest incidents underscored the need for China and the US to work towards “a new world” in which cooperation on AI safety remained possible.
“There is no way to stop AI in the current world, where there is too much economic and military motivation to go full speed [ahead],” he said, warning that this could lead to “global death”.
“The US and China are powering the AI revolution, and that gives our two nations a special responsibility … to find ways in which AI can be better governed,” Nicholas Dirks, president of the New York Academy of Sciences, said at the event on Saturday.
The experts’ remarks come ahead of two remaining meetings this year between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump, in Shenzhen and Miami, where AI governance is expected to feature prominently on the agenda.
The two countries agreed in September to establish a bilateral AI safety dialogue and incident-notification mechanism, although details of its scope and operations have yet to be disclosed.
Hellman said in his keynote speech that it would be unproductive for either China or the US to dictate AI governance policies to one another, arguing instead that the two countries needed to start working “from within”.
China and the US continue to pour trillions of dollars into AI development as they compete for dominance in a technology that carries significant geopolitical, military and economic implications.

On Friday, a commentary that appeared in the print version of the People’s Daily, mouthpiece of the ruling Communist Party, called for greater public confidence in China’s AI trajectory after claims circulated online suggesting the country was failing to use AI for productive purposes.
Some internet users in recent weeks shared figures claiming that AI use in China was concentrated in entertainment, while the US was deploying the technology in economically productive ways such as coding and knowledge-based work.
The World Laureates Forum runs through Sunday, with high-profile speakers including Z.ai chief scientist Tang Jie and Nobel Prize-winning chemist Omar Yaghi set to deliver keynote speeches about AI development on Saturday.
Additional reporting by Sherry Wang

data.title: Nearly 17,000 students hit by data leak at Hong Kong exams authority
data.description:
The personal data of nearly 17,000 mainland Chinese-based students who applied to take two international exams through the Hong Kong Examinations and Assessment Authority (HKEAA) has been leaked after its information system was compromised.
The authority said the leaked data included the names, dates of birth and email addresses of about 16,900 students. It added that there was no evidence that the Hong Kong Diploma of Secondary Education Examination (HKDSE) or any other examinations had been affected.
“The HKEAA apologises to the affected individuals and will take all feasible measures to minimise the impact of the incident on them,” it said.
The authority said the cybersecurity incident, identified on Thursday, involved an information system used for a small number of international examinations. It had reported the incident to police and notified the Office of the Privacy Commissioner for Personal Data.
It stressed that the registration systems for the HKDSE and most international examinations were separate from and independent of the compromised system.
The authority said it immediately took protective measures and launched a comprehensive investigation to determine the cause of the incident and the extent of its impact.
It had also notified the relevant examination organisation and was arranging to notify those affected.
“The HKEAA will continue to conduct a comprehensive review of the security measures for its information systems, strengthen system protection and monitoring, and take appropriate follow-up measures in light of the investigation findings,” it said.
The privacy commissioner said it had launched an investigation into the incident in accordance with established procedures.

data.title: After brutal sell-off, what comes next for the titans of Big Tech?Following disappointing quarterly earnings, tech giants face wide-ranging challenges, even as AI revenue builds.
data.description:
Soaring artificial intelligence revenues have failed to shield Intel, Amazon and Google’s parent company Alphabet from a brutal Wall Street sell-off, as their latest quarterly results deepened investor jitters over mounting capital spending and delayed returns.
Intel plunged about 23 per cent in extended trading on Thursday, while Amazon shed 7.3 per cent. Alphabet tumbled 12.6 per cent during the regular session in its worst day on record, dragging the Nasdaq Composite down 1.4 per cent and sliding slightly further after hours.
Their earnings reports exposed the precarious economics of the AI boom: hyperscalers are racing to build out advanced computing capacity well before those assets generate enough cash to finance the next wave of infrastructure.
With both Alphabet and Amazon signalling even larger capital expenditure in 2027, any slower-than-expected top-line growth threatens to squeeze liquidity while depreciation and operational costs pile up.
Ahead of the financial results, Melissa Otto, global head at S&P Visible Alpha Research, warned on Wednesday that cloud giants’ spending was “projected to outpace revenue growth in the near term”, potentially weighing on free cash flow.
Alphabet burns cash despite cloud surge
Alphabet’s Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to US$30.7 billion, while group operating profit rose by 30 per cent. But capital expenditure of US$51.4 billion outpaced operating cash flow of US$42.3 billion, leaving a quarterly free cash outflow of US$9.1 billion.
While free cash flow remained positive on a trailing 12-month basis, this marked the US giant’s second consecutive quarter recording negative free cash flow.
Liquidity was further constrained by a US$5.2 billion European Commission antitrust fine and inventory commitments for tensor processing units, which Google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said were backed by signed customer contracts.
Alphabet maintained its full-year capital expenditure forecast of US$195 billion to US$205 billion. Finance chief Anat Ashkenazi warned spending would rise substantially in 2027, driving up depreciation costs, while greater use of third-party computing infrastructure would pressure near-term cloud margins.
Compounding the pressure, core search growth slowed to 12 per cent year on year, down from 17 per cent in the second quarter and 19 per cent in the first.
While chief business officer Philipp Schindler blamed currency swings and the lower monetisation of Google AI Mode queries for the deceleration from the second quarter, the numbers fed into worries that the firm’s main revenue engine is losing momentum as online users turn to AI to search for information.
Amazon defends record capital demands
Amazon struck a parallel chord of operational strength eclipsed by capital needs. Amazon Web Services (AWS) revenue grew 39.3 per cent to US$46 billion, its fastest expansion in nearly five years, propelling its group operating margin to a record 13.9 per cent.
Yet heavy AI investment drained cash balances. Amazon posted a US$42.4 billion free cash outflow for the 12 months ending September 30, reversing a US$14.8 billion inflow a year earlier, even as operating cash flow rose 29 per cent to US$168.3 billion.
The company held its full-year cash capital expenditure guidance at about US$220 billion. Amazon CEO Andy Jassy signalled that 2027 spending would be “meaningfully more”, while pushing back against investor scepticism, saying: “We can fund this plan.”
While AWS revenue exceeded consensus estimates, it missed the 42 per cent threshold anticipated by the most bullish analysts. Looking past the near-term cash burn, Jassy projected AWS growth would exceed 40 per cent across both 2027 and 2028.
Intel hit by forecast miss and plant disruptions
Intel faced a distinct set of operational headwinds, issuing fourth-quarter guidance that missed Wall Street targets across the board. The chipmaker projected revenue of US$15 billion to US$16 billion and adjusted earnings per share of 25 US cents, well below the consensus forecasts of US$17 billion and 43 US cents cited by Goldman Sachs.
While third-quarter sales in Intel’s data centre and AI unit surged 78 per cent, revenue in its Client Computing and Physical AI Group, which includes personal computer chips, fell 5 per cent. Management said higher memory prices and limited enterprise IT budgets were denting PC demand, projecting a 10 per cent decline in global PC shipments in 2027.
Manufacturing and packaging constraints also capped server-chip deliveries. An accident at its Kiryat Gat fabrication facility in Israel was expected to shave fourth-quarter revenue by about US$300 million, with a similar drag likely in the subsequent quarter, Intel said.
Microsoft defies the hyperscaler cash drain
Microsoft, on the other hand, appeared more adept at funding heavy infrastructure out of its operations than its Big Tech peers.
Microsoft Azure revenue rose 48 per cent as operating cash flow hit US$58 billion. That comfortably absorbed US$39.4 billion in property and equipment spending, leaving the software giant with US$18.6 billion in free cash flow for the September quarter.
Chief financial officer Amy Hood reiterated that Microsoft expected to stay free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027. She noted that December-quarter capital outlays would eclipse US$50 billion, inclusive of finance leases. Some third-party capacity deliveries had shifted to the fiscal second half.

data.title: Hong Kong woman, 66, loses HK$2.7 million in money-laundering phone scam
data.description:
A 66-year-old Hong Kong woman was swindled out of HK$2.7 million (US$344,158) in a phone scam after a caller alleged that her bank account had been involved in money laundering.
Police said the woman, who lives in Sau Mau Ping, told the force at about 5am on Saturday that she had received the call earlier this month from a suspected scammer.
He claimed her bank account, the one she used to buy insurance online, had been involved in money laundering and allegedly instructed her to transfer funds for investigation purposes.
The victim first transferred HK$2 million, then a further HK$700,000, into two bank accounts designated by the scammer.
She later came to suspect she had been defrauded and contacted police.
Police have classified the case as deception and no arrests have been made so far.

data.title: Xpeng says Chinese flying cars trump Tesla’s Roadster for practical use
data.description:
Flying cars developed by Chinese companies are by design more feasible for commercial use than Tesla’s Roadster, according to an executive at Xpeng, after a recent demonstration by the US tech giant sparked discussion about tech leadership in mainland China.
Wang Tan, co-founder of Aridge, the affiliate of Chinese electric vehicle (EV) maker Xpeng, said Chinese companies had adopted different technologies than Tesla did.
While the Roadster’s mid-air flip and successful landing as seen in a live stream earlier this month was impressive, its jet-like configuration required high-pressure storage tanks, which severely limited cabin seating and application environments, Tan said.
Moreover, the Roadster’s flight time was limited to a few seconds as the cold-gas pressure in the storage tanks depletes rapidly, whereas an Xpeng aircraft can stay in the air for about 20 minutes, Wang told the South China Morning Post in an interview on Thursday.
“I think that in the future, [Roadster] may not serve as a vehicle for air travel,” said Wang. “But what we’re developing, it’s foreseeable that it will be able to fly for longer periods and become a viable mode of transport.”
The adoption of different technologies is the key reason. Aridge, formerly known as AeroHT, employed multiple rotors in its flying car which enabled it to hover while the high-density battery supported a longer flight, Wang noted.
Xpeng’s Land Aircraft Carrier, which combines an aircraft and an off-road vehicle as a power bank, has the potential to expand the application beyond sightseeing to emergency rescue and industrial maintenance in offshore wind farms or oil platforms, he added.

Besides the multirotor configuration used by Xpeng, the electric aircraft developed by Shanghai Volant Aerotech and Aerofugia, a sister company of Geely Auto Group, use compound wings and a tilt-rotor, respectively, which can ensure higher speeds or longer flight times in the commercialisation stage.
The successful flight of Tesla’s Roadster triggered a debate on Chinese social media over whether the US tech giant was ahead of its Chinese rivals in flying car technology, with state media including Communist Party mouthpiece the People’s Daily calling for confidence in the country’s EV industry.
Xpeng chairman and CEO He Xiaopeng said in a post on his personal WeChat account that although Roadster provided a new solution, the feasibility of all flying cars was still subject to safety, security, flying times, and regulatory certification.
Wang said he expected Xpeng’s aircraft to achieve even longer flight times in future as battery energy density increased and lightweight materials continued to be improved, which would be the “biggest difference” from Tesla’s Roadster.
“Once [flying cars] start serving a more practical purpose, it may go from being a fun toy to becoming a tool,” Wang concluded.
However, Wang acknowledged that Xpeng’s application for a safety approval certificate issued by the Civil Aviation Administration of China was proceeding slower than expected.
But he pledged that the firm would double down on proving the product’s safety to win a regulatory nod.
Carrying a price tag of 2 million yuan (US$300,000), Xpeng has received more than 7,000 orders from around the world since presales launched in December 2024.
Aridge delivered its first Land Aircraft Carrier to the United Arab Emirates earlier this month, according to an announcement on October 20.
However, as Chinese certification is also required for overseas sales, the aircraft cannot be legally flown by customers yet.

data.title: Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi’s remains found in soup pots and fridge, court told
data.description:
Slain Hong Kong socialite Abby Choi Tin-fung’s remains were stored in two soup pots and a refrigerator after her body was dismembered with an electric saw in a rural village flat, a court has heard.
The High Court trial took a turn towards the end of its fifth week when Choi’s former father-in-law, Kwong Kau, changed his plea to guilty on a charge of illegally disposing of her body. His admission came after the court heard how some of the 28-year-old’s remains were found in Lung Mei village in Tai Po on February 24, 2023.
Kwong, a 68-year-old retired police officer, remains on trial for murder alongside his two sons, Anthony Kwong Kong-kit, 35, and Choi’s ex-husband, Alex Kwong Kong-chi, 31. Both sons pleaded guilty to preventing Choi’s burial before the trial began in late September.
Light-hearted exchanges between the judge and lawyers occasionally eased the sombre atmosphere in court, but Deputy Judge Brian Keith reminded the nine-member jury to remain serious throughout the proceedings.
“A young woman died in what was said to be tragic circumstances, and that should not be forgotten,” Keith said.
Detective Constable Chan Wai-hung said police broke into the 600 sq ft rented flat after investigators identified a white Toyota Alphard parked outside as the vehicle used to transport Choi on February 21.
Chan described an “overwhelming” smell of air freshener, similar to that of public toilets, as he entered the flat. Its windows were completely covered with black tape.
In a bedroom covered with blue plastic sheets, police found a plastic box containing a wooden chopping board and what appeared to be human flesh and internal organs, the court heard.
Chan said he later found Choi’s legs in two rubbish bags inside a refrigerator in the living room.

Police also seized two soup pots. One was found to contain Choi’s head when examined at a public mortuary.
Under cross-examination, Chan denied tampering with evidence and said the four colleagues who accompanied him had not touched anything during the search.
Another officer, Sergeant Lam Chun, denied using excessive force when arresting Alex Kwong on February 25 or failing to label DNA samples taken from him properly after his arrest.
Senior government chemist Dr Tam Cheok-ning, a specialist in tool mark analysis, said he found a cut mark on Choi’s remains consistent with the blade of one of two electric saws seized from the flat.
Prosecutors said Choi went missing on February 21 after boarding the Toyota Alphard driven by Anthony Kwong, believing he would take her to Pak Shek Kok to collect her eight-year-old daughter from school.
Alex Kwong allegedly sat beside Choi in the back seat and struck her on the head with a hammer during the journey. Police seized a one-pound ball-peen hammer from the village flat three days later.
A hardware shop employee in Kowloon City confirmed that the hammer seized from the flat was the one he sold to Anthony Kwong on February 15.
In a written statement, Alex Kwong’s friend and former business partner Herman Ng Deng-hao said the defendant had asked to borrow a car in January 2023. Kwong said his own car was booked in for maintenance and he needed a vehicle to drive his children to school.
Ng referred Kwong to his own elder brother, who lent the latter a seven-seater Toyota Alphard. Kwong allegedly used the vehicle to transport equipment for dismembering Choi’s body after she was killed. It was not the Alphard she had used.
The statement also shed light on Alex Kwong’s apparent affluent lifestyle while he was living in mainland China and evading criminal proceedings in Hong Kong over a HK$6.3 million theft case.

He said Kwong appeared wealthy during his time on the mainland, staying at the luxury Rosewood Guangzhou hotel and using a personal driver to travel around the province in either a Rolls-Royce saloon or a seven-seater Lexus.
But whenever they met for meals, Ng noted, Kwong appeared to use mobile payment apps authenticated under the abbreviated names “Fung” or “Tin-fung”.
Ng said Kwong was forced to return to Hong Kong on June 10, 2022, after telling Choi he had a girlfriend.
According to Ng, the influencer was upset that her ex-husband was “picking up girls” on the mainland while neglecting their two children in Hong Kong.
Prosecutors allege the murder stemmed from a family feud over the proposed sale of a HK$72 million (US$9.2 million) flat at the upmarket Kadooria residential estate in Ho Man Tin.
Kwong Kau, the flat’s registered owner, allegedly resented Choi’s efforts to sell it and enlisted his two sons to help kill his former daughter-in-law and dispose of her body.
The court heard that the elder Kwong signed a power of attorney on November 7, 2022, authorising Choi to negotiate the sale after her mother threatened to take him to court.
Two property agents who were contacted by Choi in November 2022 and February 2023, respectively, testified that she was eager to sell the flat. They said no prospective buyers had made inquiries about it before her death.
The trial continues.

data.title: Evergrande liquidators strike US$513 million deal to sell property services arm
data.description:
Liquidators of China Evergrande Group have agreed to sell a controlling stake in its property management arm to investment firm PAG for HK$4.03 billion (US$513.6 million), as they seek to recover assets for creditors owed US$46 billion.
The sale of a 51.016 per cent stake in Evergrande Property Services could give the profitable business a new controlling shareholder after its parent used billions of yuan of its bank deposits as collateral for loans, leaving the company struggling to recover the money.
PAG, a Hong Kong-based investment firm, would acquire about 5.52 billion shares from China Evergrande and CEG Holdings, both in liquidation, according to a joint announcement on Friday.
“Following an extensive and competitive sale process, we are pleased to have been able to conclude this agreement with PAG, the completion of which will enable [Evergrande Property Services] to move onwards into a renewed phase of growth,” liquidator Eddie Middleton said in a statement to the South China Morning Post.
Further work was required before the transaction could be completed, Middleton added.
PAG will pay HK$0.8359 per share for China Evergrande’s 147.16 million shares and HK$0.7271 per share for CEG Holdings’ 5.37 billion shares. The transaction remains subject to conditions, including regulatory approval in mainland China.
Upon completion, PAG will be required to make an unconditional mandatory cash offer for the remaining shares at HK$0.8359 apiece. The offer price is 29.5 per cent below Evergrande Property Services’ closing price of HK$1.185 on October 28, the last trading day before the announcement.
Following a brief suspension ahead of the takeover announcement, the company resumed trading on Friday.
PAG said it intended to maintain Evergrande Property Services’ Hong Kong listing and did not plan any major operational changes beyond board-level adjustments, according to the statement.
The property manager provides services across mainland China and reported revenue of 6.94 billion yuan (US$1 billion) and net profit of 503 million yuan in the first half of 2026.
Its finances, however, have been caught in its parent’s collapse. China Evergrande used 13.4 billion yuan of its bank deposits as collateral for loans. By June, Evergrande Property Services had recovered just 9.5 million yuan from its parent and other parties, according to its interim report.
China Evergrande defaulted on its offshore debt in 2021 and was ordered to wind up by Hong Kong’s High Court in January 2024. Its liquidators had recovered US$435.9 million through asset sales and loan recoveries, less than 1 per cent of the US$46 billion in creditor claims, according to their second progress report published earlier this month.

data.title: From digital pets to robot pals: how AI is changing Hong Kong classrooms
data.description:
Hands shot up in a Hong Kong Primary Two classroom as pupils debated what their digital pet needed more, meal vouchers or the latest game cards.
Their teacher at SKH Kei Oi Primary School in Sham Shui Po had created the virtual pet using artificial intelligence (AI) and web tools for a lesson on saving and budgeting.
With each spending decision, the pet’s mood and savings changed on screen, helping pupils discover the consequences of careless spending.
Such lessons are becoming more common across Hong Kong, where about 60 per cent of primary and secondary schools use AI in teaching or administration, according to an Education University of Hong Kong survey released in June.
Supported by a government blueprint for digital education and a HK$500,000 (US$63,733) grant for each publicly funded school, schools are developing their own AI platforms or working with industry to adapt the technology to their students’ needs.
AI has helped teachers plan lessons and overcome barriers to learning. But teachers said assessing students’ AI-assisted work required more training, while principals called for closer collaboration between schools and industry to support pupils with special educational needs.
The Education Bureau released its Blueprint for Digital Education Development in June, requiring teachers to complete at least 30 hours of digital training every three years and directing schools to incorporate AI strategies into their annual development plans.
The bureau has also provided a one-off HK$500,000 grant to every publicly funded primary and secondary school through its AI for Empowering Learning and Teaching Funding Programme, launched in 2025. The money can be used to buy or lease AI software, hardware and platforms, and to fund activities that develop students’ AI literacy.
SKH Kei Oi Primary School has adopted both off-the-shelf and custom-built AI tools, initially focusing on science and English for Primary Four to Six pupils.
Ready-made applications include image generators that turn pupils’ English compositions into comics, as well as platforms that assess their speaking and writing skills.
Principal Szeto Kar-ying said finding suitable products in a crowded market was not easy, but the school’s guiding principle was to put teaching needs ahead of the latest technology.
When no suitable product is available, the school works with industry to develop its own solution.
With support from a programme run by the bureau and Cyberport, it partnered with a technology company to create an AI-driven science reading platform that guides pupils through texts and concepts.
“Funding goes first to projects that fit curriculum needs and can be sustained and scaled up. We also encourage our teachers to experiment with AI in everyday teaching and classroom activities,” Szeto said.
Teacher Cynthia Doo Chi-yin’s budgeting game, in which her Primary Two humanities class manages a digital pet’s monthly spending, is one example of teachers developing their own AI teaching tools.
“I make the spending choices together with them in class. They are excited to explore it first-hand and discover on their own that irrational spending has consequences, affecting the character’s mood,” she said.
While AI has opened up new possibilities for lesson design, it has also made assessing students’ abilities more challenging.
“If we only assess the final product, students can easily get AI to do the work for them. Assessment should value the process over the result and cover how students collaborate with AI, not just test their knowledge,” said Chan Yuk, the school’s IT coordinator.
He said this approach added to teachers’ workloads, and schools needed to provide training and time rather than leaving staff to work it out themselves.
Dragan Gasevic, chair professor in the Faculty of Education and the School of Computing and Data Science at the University of Hong Kong, said assessments now needed to shift their focus from the final product to the process behind it.
“When a sprinter races, the coach does not just record the finishing time. They replay the whole race step by step to find the moments where performance could improve,” he said.
“We need tools that let teachers and students replay these steps too, and identify the points of weakness when students interact with AI.”
Such tools should be co-designed with children and teachers, he said, with students given control over their own data and schools fostering a coaching culture.
Gasevic said schools needed to distinguish AI designed for education from general-purpose AI.
“Real learning gains require specialised adaptive systems, not simply asking ChatGPT or Gemini to run a Socratic dialogue. These systems, built on more than 50 years of research in AI in education, need components that adapt to the individual needs of each student,” he said.

For students with special educational needs, AI can help overcome learning barriers by responding to their emotional needs and offering alternatives to typing, such as pictures and voice input.
Hong Chi Winifred Mary Cheung Morninghope School, which caters to children aged six to 18 with intellectual disabilities, has introduced various robots as learning companions.
Principal Chu Pui-man said the school had invested in smart devices and AI platforms to immerse students in technology and help them become confident using it in daily life beyond school.
“We bought two humanoid robots that students can learn to programme, and they once led the whole school in morning exercise,” she said.
“In our classrooms we keep more than 10 companion robots, our AI learning buddies, which chat with students when they feel unhappy and comfort them.”
The school has also partnered with a technology company to create an AI avatar that serves as an assistant on students’ tablets. Because commercial products do not meet all its students’ needs, it maintains an in-house team to develop a school-based platform.
“Our students might not speak fast or clearly, so we need to adjust the platform to their pace, guide them step by step and not rush ahead, and allow them to enlarge the text. We also preset question choices on the platform for students who cannot type,” she said.
She added that AI also allowed students to ask questions through images or speech rather than using a conventional keyboard.
But customising and trialling AI products took additional time and money.
“We hope to see cross-school resource sharing and centralised procurement for special education, so schools do not each end up buying the same thing at a high price,” she said.
“If the tech industry could recommend well-tested products and explain why they suit our students, we could save time searching and customising on our own.”
The task of matching products to schools falls partly to Hong Kong Education City (EdCity), the government-funded education portal.
Launched in 2000 to promote the digitalisation of education, EdCity has evolved in recent years from primarily a repository of digital content into a platform connecting technology companies with schools as AI use grows.
Its executive director, Dr Tenny Lam Fung, said schools could draw on AI solutions from around the world. For mainstream schools, the challenge lay in choosing the right ones.
“Mainstream schools have many choices. The question is which one to pick, how to use it, and how to get clear feedback. We provide a platform, EdMarket, for schools and companies to share their successful cases and help schools choose,” he said.
For special schools, the challenge worked both ways: schools had fewer suitable products to choose from, while companies struggled to reach the right classrooms.
“Students with special needs have many different learning needs, and it is very hard for one solution to meet them all. So the challenge for special schools is how to find the right solution for each application context,” he said.
He added that EdCity had stepped up support for special schools, including through an AI in Education Forum co-organised with the Education University of Hong Kong, at which special education researchers present their work.
Lam described the digital education blueprint as an important milestone in setting the overall direction but said choosing solutions was a matter of implementation for schools and the Education Bureau.
“The blueprint sets out the framework, principles and policies. It will not go into detail on how to choose solutions. That is where execution comes in, and that is the role we play,” he said.
“In execution, things must keep evolving as technology updates. But some principles will remain unchanged: people first, technology for good and using technology responsibly.”

data.title: AI, fuelled by advanced chips, set to power their manufacture: industry veteran
data.description:
Artificial intelligence is no longer merely the driving force behind global semiconductor demand, but is also actively reinventing how chips are designed and built, industry leaders and scientists said at a major science forum in Shanghai on Friday.
Chen Yunji, co-founder of AI chipmaker Cambricon Technologies, predicted that the integration between AI and chip design would eventually automate the chip design process entirely.
“In the [next] 10 years, the most important development … is the RSI (recursive self-improvement) techniques for artificial intelligence, where AI models improve AI models, and AI chips improve AI chips,” Chen said.
“With the potential of RSI, it is possible that one day AI systems will autonomously design better chips, which leads to better AI systems in a self-recursive loop.”
The transformation is already reaching the factory floor, according to the speakers. Lu Guangquan, chairman of Chinese semiconductor equipment maker Piotech, said industrial AI had evolved from generating text to executing physical fabrication processes.
With front-end manufacturing tools accounting for over 80 per cent of fabrication costs, Chinese foundries were increasingly deploying AI-powered digital twins and predictive models to improve chip equipment engineering and operations, and eventually boost wafer yields, Lu said.
The remarks, delivered at the 2026 World Laureates Forum, underscored how China’s chip sector is embracing AI to overcome domestic manufacturing bottlenecks and drive automation across the entire supply chain.
The shift comes as AI shapes the architecture of scientific computing. Jack Dongarra, an American computing pioneer and Turing Award winner who also addressed the forum, said AI was forcing those in the industry to rethink processor design.

“AI does not simply add another workload to high-performance computing; it also changes the hardware that scientific computing will have,” Dongarra said, noting that AI workloads depended less on 64-bit FP64 calculations and placed greater strain on memory bandwidth and energy across systems.
FP64 is a 64-bit double-precision floating point, the mathematical format that most scientific simulations and supercomputing benchmarks rely on.
Beyond the production line, the technology was reshaping how China trained its next generation of chip engineers, experts said.
Wu Hanming, director of the Information Science Division at Zhejiang University, said the university’s integrated circuits college was using AI systems such as FabGPT alongside simulation engines. The set-up created virtual fabs where students could experience CMOS production lines digitally, he said.
But even as AI automated code and semiconductor layouts, it remained dependent on hardware to perceive the real world, according to Liu Sheng, dean of the School of Integrated Circuits at Wuhan University.
Liu highlighted surging demand for smart sensors and micro-electromechanical systems (MEMS) in humanoid robotics and autonomous driving.
“Sensors are the foundation … acting as the link between the physical and information worlds,” Liu said, adding that developing advanced packaging and testing platforms was critical to keeping complex MEMS chips reliable and cost-effective.

data.title: On This Day|Fire at Hong Kong’s Jumbo Floating Restaurant kills 34 in 1971 – SCMP archive
data.description:
This story was first published on October 31, 1971.
Aberdeen was yesterday (October 30, 1971) rocked by a tremendous explosion followed by fire which swept through the $14 million Jumbo Restaurant, killing 13 and injuring at least 42 others on board.
It happened so quickly that within five minutes, fire engulfed the four-decked floating restaurant, reducing it to a charred hulk.
Hundreds of people leapt for life from the decks and from the pagoda-shaped towers of the palatial restaurant.
It was a frantic scene of struggle for survival which grasped boat people and weekend yachtsmen nearby who watched in horror.
The news of the fire and the high toll shocked Aberdeen.

Just how hard the blow was to the fishing community could not be immediately ascertained, as a large number of the casualties are believed to come from Aberdeen itself.
Cause of the high toll was the presence on board of 200 painters, welders and workers putting the finishing touches for the opening of the restaurant scheduled for November 17.
The Chief Fire Officer, Mr H. T. J. Hutchins, who directed the fire fighting operations, attributed the high toll to the rapid spread of the fire, coupled with a series of explosions, and the difficulties in getting out.
“The only exit is jumping into the sea,” the Chief Officer, Hongkong, said.
The water was full of bobbing heads, and boats of all descriptions rushed to pick them up.
One of the early parties who dashed to the scene was six police officers from Aberdeen.
They were Detective Inspector James Bruce, Blue Beret Inspector P. M. Mullens, and Detective Inspector L. Burton, Cpl Lam Kam-yat and two constables.
They spotted the fire from the station, and rushed to nearby boats for the rescue.
“A dozen of them were clinging to the sides of the Jumbo restaurant,” Insp Bruce said.
“They were badly burned and were shouting for help,” he said.
After picking up these survivors, the police officers continued the rescue work in the vicinity picking up more people.
Several sampans near the floating restaurant were not spared from the holocaust.
Four children of a boat family were burned to death when their craft caught fire and was completely gutted.
Their grief-stricken father, Wong Fat-hoi, 46, told the police of the tragedy after he helped his wife ashore.
The children were left on the boat when Mr Wong and three other members of his family were ashore.
When he and his wife heard of the fire, they rushed back only to find the four had perished.
Mrs Wong who collapsed on hearing the news was rushed to hospital.
A fisherman, Mr Chan Kan-tai, 23, tried desperately to row to his boat where his mother-in-law and several children were but the intense heat and leaping flames forced him to turn back.
The family had all jumped safely into the water, and only his mother-in-law was hurt with burns in the back, Mr Chan later learned.

Mr Chang Ching-sing, one of the restaurant’s stewards who escaped, said the fire broke out at the stern on the lowest deck of the ship at about 3 pm.
Welding was being carried out in the section of the ship, he said.
The fire quickly swept through the whole craft.
“Everyone had to jump as the fire was burning fiercely,” he said.
A yachtswoman who witnessed the start of the fire, said many workers on the upper decks who went to the stern to have a look soon found themselves trapped as the fire rapidly spread upwards.
Mr Hutchins said his men removed 61 casualties to hospital. Police launches might have picked up more, he said.
He believed the fire started as a result of an explosion apparently from a large quantity of oil and a number of oxy-acetylene tubes on board.
Investigations into the disaster had already begun, Mr Hutchins said.
The Acting Governor, Sir Hugh Norman-Walker, last night sent his sympathy to the families of the victims.
In a message from Government House, Sir Hugh said he was shocked to learn of the tragic news.
